## Proof

**Yes.** Every closed connected subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{U}(n)$ is cut out by polynomial equations in the real and imaginary parts $x_{ij}=\operatorname{Re}(a_{ij})$, $y_{ij}=\operatorname{Im}(a_{ij})$ of the matrix entries.

---

**Setup.** Identify $M_n(\mathbb{C})\cong\mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ via $(x_{ij},y_{ij})$. The group $\mathrm{U}(n)$ is the real algebraic set defined by the polynomial equations
$$\sum_k\bigl(x_{ki}x_{kj}+y_{ki}y_{kj}\bigr)=\delta_{ij},\qquad \sum_k\bigl(y_{ki}x_{kj}-x_{ki}y_{kj}\bigr)=0,$$
expressing $AA^*=I$. Let $I(G)\subset\mathbb{R}[x_{ij},y_{ij}]$ be the ideal of polynomials vanishing on $G$, and let $Z:=V(I(G))$ be the corresponding real algebraic set (the Zariski closure of $G$). We prove $Z=G$.

**Step 1 — $Z\subset\mathrm{U}(n)$, hence $Z$ is compact.** Since $G\subset\mathrm{U}(n)$, every polynomial vanishing on $\mathrm{U}(n)$ vanishes on $G$, i.e. $I(\mathrm{U}(n))\subset I(G)$. Therefore
$$Z=V(I(G))\subset V(I(\mathrm{U}(n)))=\mathrm{U}(n).$$
As a closed subset of the compact set $\mathrm{U}(n)$, $Z$ is compact.

**Step 2 — $Z$ is a real algebraic subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$.** The Zariski closure of a subgroup of an algebraic group is an algebraic subgroup. Indeed, for $g\in G$, the polynomial map $x\mapsto gx$ sends $G$ into $G\subset Z$; the preimage $\{x:gx\in Z\}$ is Zariski-closed and contains $G$, hence contains $Z$, giving $gZ\subset Z$. Similarly $Zg\subset Z$, and $Z$ is closed under inverses (the map $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ on $\mathrm{GL}(n)$ is rational, equivalently use the adjugate). So $Z$ is a subgroup.

**Step 3 — $Z$ is connected.** The identity component $Z^\circ$ (Zariski topology) is a Zariski-open-and-closed subgroup containing $e$. Since $G$ is connected and contains $e$, we have $G\subset Z^\circ$. As $Z^\circ$ is Zariski-closed and contains $G$, $Z=\overline{G}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}\subset Z^\circ$, so $Z=Z^\circ$.

**Step 4 — Every representative function of $Z$ is a polynomial in $x_{ij},y_{ij}$.** Let $\rho:Z\hookrightarrow\mathrm{U}(n)$ be the faithful standard representation; its matrix coefficients are $x_{ij}$ and $y_{ij}$ (equivalently $z_{ij}$ and $\bar z_{ij}$). Let $P$ be the $*$-algebra generated by $\{x_{ij},y_{ij}\}|_Z$, i.e. by matrix coefficients of $\rho$ and $\bar\rho$. Then $P$ is a $Z\times Z$-submodule of the representative function algebra $R(Z)=\bigoplus_\pi W_\pi$ (sum over irreducibles $\pi$, each $W_\pi\cong V_\pi\otimes V_\pi^*$ irreducible under $Z\times Z$). Since $\rho$ is faithful, $P$ separates points of $Z$; by Stone–Weierstrass, $P$ is dense in $C(Z)$. As a $Z\times Z$-submodule, $P=\bigoplus_\pi(P\cap W_\pi)$ with $P\cap W_\pi\in\{0,W_\pi\}$. Density in $L^2(Z)$ forces $P\cap W_\pi=W_\pi$ for every $\pi$ (otherwise $P$ lies in a proper closed subspace). Hence $P=R(Z)$: every representative function of $Z$ is a polynomial in $x_{ij},y_{ij}$.

**Step 5 — $G=Z$.** Suppose for contradiction that $G\subsetneq Z$. Then $G$ is a proper closed subgroup of the compact connected group $Z$, so the homogeneous space $Z/G$ has more than one point. By the Peter–Weyl theorem, there exists a **non-constant** right-$G$-invariant representative function $f$ on $Z$: averaging any representative function over $G$ (Haar measure on $G$) produces a right-$G$-invariant representative function, and non-trivial such functions exist because $Z/G$ is non-trivial and representative functions are dense in $C(Z)$.

Right-$G$-invariance gives $f(g)=f(e)$ for all $g\in G$, so the polynomial $f-f(e)$ vanishes on $G$, i.e. $f-f(e)\in I(G)$. But $f$ is non-constant on $Z$, so $f-f(e)$ does **not** vanish on all of $Z$, i.e. $f-f(e)\notin I(Z)$.

This contradicts $I(G)=I(Z)$, which holds because $G\subset Z$ gives $I(Z)\subset I(G)$, while $Z=V(I(G))$ gives $I(G)\subset I(V(I(G)))=I(Z)$. Hence $G=Z$.

**Conclusion.** Since $G=Z=V(I(G))$ and $I(G)\subset\mathbb{R}[x_{ij},y_{ij}]$ is finitely generated (Hilbert basis theorem), $G$ is defined by finitely many polynomial equations in the real and imaginary parts of the matrix entries. $\blacksquare$
